name: The Time Study: Is AI Actually Saving Time?
title: The Time Study: Is AI Actually Saving Time?
answer: The time study is a simple before and after check on whether an AI tool actually saves teachers time. It matters because schools often adopt tools on the promise of time savings, yet a review of 63 studies found that 46 percent found no evidence that automatic feedback eased instructors' workload (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). Without measuring, leaders cannot know whether the tool helps or where any saved time goes.

sections.body: Schools frequently bring in AI tools because they are said to save teachers time, but few check whether that happens. The time study solves this by measuring how long key tasks take before a tool is introduced and again after a few weeks of use. It captures the real time saved, including the time teachers spend checking and fixing AI output. It also asks where any saved time goes, because saved time can be absorbed by other demands. This gives leaders a factual basis for deciding whether a tool is worth keeping and how to protect any benefit.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Before introducing a tool, teachers record how long tasks such as planning a week of lessons or grading a set of essays take. After a few weeks of using the tool, they record the same tasks again. The difference shows the real time saved, including time spent checking and fixing AI output. Teachers also record what they did with any time saved, such as more small group teaching, more feedback conferences, or leaving earlier. A Google Form makes this easy, with teachers logging tasks and times each week in a few minutes, and the results are shared with teachers rather than used to judge them; the text also mentions a primary school study where saved time was often absorbed by other demands (Carson et al., 2026).
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text does not give a formal evidence label for this idea. It cites a review of 63 studies of automatic feedback, which found that many showed benefits for students, but 46 percent found no evidence that it eased instructors' workload (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). It also cites a primary school study, which found that saved time was often absorbed by other demands (Carson et al., 2026). These findings support the book's point that time savings cannot be assumed.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that time savings cannot be assumed, so a tool should not be kept just because it promises to save time. Saved time may also be absorbed by other demands, which means leaders need to know where it goes if they want to protect it. The time study should be shared with teachers and must not be used to judge them or to monitor individual teachers. The purpose is to learn whether tools help, not to evaluate people. Decisions about whether a tool helps and how saved time is used remain with teachers and school leaders, not with the tool.
